prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

WASHINGTON (CNN) -- The Iraq war has strained U.S. forces to the point where they could not fight another large-scale war, according to a survey of military officers. U.S. troops patrol Haifa Street in Baghdad last week. Of those surveyed, 88 percent believe the demands of the Iraq war have "stretched the U.S. military dangerously thin." On the other hand, 56 percent of the officers disagree that the war has "broken" the military. Eighty percent of officers believe it is unreasonable to expect the U.S. military to wage another major war successfully at present. Foreign Policy magazine and the Center for a New American Security on Tuesday issued the U.S. Military Index, a survey of 3,400 present and former U.S. military officers. "We asked the officers whether they thought the U.S. military was stronger or weaker than it was five years ago," said Michael Boyer, who helped write the report. "Sixty percent said the U.S. military is weaker than it was five years ago," Boyer told reporters. The report found that officers "see a military apparatus severely strained by the grinding demands of war." More than half of the officers responding cited the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan, and the "pace of troop deployments" needed for those conflicts, the survey said. The report comes a few weeks before the five-year anniversary of the Iraq war, where a troop "surge" is winding down by summer. The U.S. military is proposing a pause in troop reductions for a period of review before any more decisions on withdrawals. The officers have "an overwhelmingly negative view" of many of the early decisions shaping the Iraq war, but most believe the present U.S. counterinsurgency strategy and troop increases are good omens for success in Iraq. A majority of officers in the Iraq war say some policy decisions have "hindered the prospects for success there." "These include shortening the time units spend at home between deployments and accepting more recruits who do not meet the military's standards. Even the military's ability to care for some of its own -- mentally wounded soldiers and veterans -- was judged by most officers to be substandard," the survey found. At the same time, 64 percent of the officers believe morale in the military remains high. Nearly three-quarters of the officers believe civilian leaders set "unreasonable goals for the military in post-Saddam Iraq." "They believe more troops were needed on the ground at the start of the fighting. They believe disbanding the Iraqi military was a mistake," the survey said. However, nearly nine of 10 think the surge and Gen. David Petraeus' counterinsurgency strategy are "raising the U.S. military's chance for success there." The officers believe "that either China or Iran, not the United States, is emerging as the strategic victor" in the Iraq war. "The United States has been preoccupied away from Asia," said Kurt Campbell, the head of the group that conducted the survey. China's rising influence worldwide predates the war but is part of a "great game under way in Asia for influence, for relationships," Campbell said. The U.S. focus on Iraq "sends a message to our friends and others that maybe we're not as focused on the drama that's playing out there," he said. Iran has gained from the war because of the removal of Iraq "as a strategic counterweight," the report said. The survey portrayed Iran, the Taiwan Strait (where tensions have flared between China and Taiwan), Syria and North Korea as four potential hot spots and sought opinions of how prepared the U.S. is "to successfully fight a major combat operation there." Officers were asked to judge the preparedness of the U.S. on a scale of one to 10, with 10 meaning "fully prepared" and one indicating "unable to execute." Iran was rated 4.5, the Taiwan Strait ( where there have been tensions between China and Taiwan) 4.9, Syria 5.1, and North Korea 4.7. The officers ranked the Navy and Air Force readiness the highest at 6.8 and 6.6, respectively. The Army and Marines, which have assumed the "bulk of the burden in Iraq and Afghanistan," ranked 4.7 and 5.7, respectively. Other results of the survey: .

outputs.L1:
WASHINGTON (CNN) — The war in Iraq has strained U.S. forces to the point that they would be unable to fight another large-scale conflict, according to a survey of military officers.

U.S. troops patrolled Haifa Street in Baghdad last week.

Among those surveyed, 88 percent said they believe the demands of the Iraq war have “stretched the U.S. military dangerously thin.” At the same time, 56 percent of officers disagreed with the assertion that the war has “broken” the military. Eighty percent said they believe it is unreasonable to expect the U.S. military to successfully wage another major war at present.

Foreign Policy magazine and the Center for a New American Security on Tuesday released the U.S. Military Index, a survey of 3,400 current and former U.S. military officers.

“We asked the officers whether they thought the U.S. military was stronger or weaker than it was five years ago,” said Michael Boyer, who helped write the report. “Sixty percent said the U.S. military is weaker than it was five years ago,” Boyer told reporters.

The report found that officers “see a military apparatus severely strained by the grinding demands of war.” More than half of the officers who responded cited the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan, as well as the “pace of troop deployments” required for those conflicts, the survey said.

The report comes just weeks before the fifth anniversary of the Iraq war, as a troop “surge” is set to wind down by summer. The U.S. military is proposing a pause in troop reductions to allow for a period of review before any further decisions on withdrawals are made.

The officers expressed “an overwhelmingly negative view” of many of the early decisions that shaped the Iraq war, although most said they believe the current U.S. counterinsurgency strategy and troop increases are promising signs for success in Iraq.

A majority of officers surveyed about the Iraq war said some policy decisions have “hindered the prospects for success there.”

“These include shortening the time units spend at home between deployments and accepting more recruits who do not meet the military’s standards. Even the military’s ability to care for some of its own — mentally wounded soldiers and veterans — was judged by most officers to be substandard,” the survey found.

At the same time, 64 percent of officers said they believe morale in the military remains high.

Nearly three-quarters of the officers said civilian leaders set “unreasonable goals for the military in post-Saddam Iraq.”

“They believe more troops were needed on the ground at the start of the fighting. They believe disbanding the Iraqi military was a mistake,” the survey said.

However, nearly nine in 10 said they believe the surge and Gen. David Petraeus’ counterinsurgency strategy are “raising the U.S. military’s chance for success there.”

The officers said they believe “that either China or Iran, not the United States, is emerging as the strategic victor” in the Iraq war.

“The United States has been preoccupied away from Asia,” said Kurt Campbell, head of the group that conducted the survey.

China’s rising influence worldwide predates the war but is part of a “great game under way in Asia for influence, for relationships,” Campbell said.

The U.S. focus on Iraq “sends a message to our friends and others that maybe we’re not as focused on the drama that’s playing out there,” he said.

Iran has benefited from the war because of the removal of Iraq “as a strategic counterweight,” the report said.

The survey identified Iran, the Taiwan Strait, Syria and North Korea as four potential hot spots and sought officers’ views on how prepared the United States is “to successfully fight a major combat operation there.” The Taiwan Strait was noted as an area where tensions have flared between China and Taiwan.

Officers were asked to assess U.S. preparedness on a scale of one to 10, with 10 meaning “fully prepared” and one indicating “unable to execute.” Iran was rated 4.5; the Taiwan Strait, 4.9; Syria, 5.1; and North Korea, 4.7.

The officers ranked Navy and Air Force readiness the highest, at 6.8 and 6.6, respectively. The Army and Marines, which have borne the “bulk of the burden in Iraq and Afghanistan,” were ranked at 4.7 and 5.7, respectively.

Other results of the survey:

WASHINGTON (CNN) — A poll of military officers indicates that the war in Iraq has placed such heavy pressure on American forces that they would not currently be capable of conducting another major war. U.S. service members were seen patrolling Haifa Street in Baghdad the previous week.

Among those questioned, 88 percent said the requirements of the Iraq conflict have left the U.S. armed forces “dangerously thin.” However, 56 percent rejected the idea that the war has “broken” the military. At the same time, 80 percent said it would be unrealistic to expect the United States military to successfully fight another large war right now.

Foreign Policy magazine and the Center for a New American Security released the U.S. Military Index on Tuesday. The report was based on a survey of 3,400 current and former U.S. military officers.

Michael Boyer, who contributed to the report, said the survey asked officers whether they considered the military stronger or weaker than it had been five years earlier. “Sixty percent said the U.S. military is weaker than it was five years ago,” Boyer told journalists.

According to the report, officers described a defense establishment under extreme pressure from the continuing demands of war. The survey said more than half of respondents pointed to the conflicts in Iraq and Afghanistan, along with the tempo of troop deployments required for those wars.

The findings were released just weeks before the fifth anniversary of the Iraq war. The troop “surge” in Iraq was expected to wind down by the summer. U.S. military leaders were recommending a pause in further troop cuts so they could review the situation before making additional withdrawal decisions.

The officers expressed a strongly negative assessment of many early choices that shaped the Iraq conflict. Still, most said the current U.S. counterinsurgency approach and the added troop levels were positive signs for possible success in Iraq.

Most officers who served in the Iraq war said certain policy choices had damaged the chances of success there. The survey identified examples such as reducing the amount of time units spend at home between deployments and allowing more recruits who fail to meet military standards. It also found that most officers considered the military’s care for some of its own personnel — including psychologically injured troops and veterans — to be below acceptable standards.

Even so, 64 percent of the officers said morale across the military remains strong.

Almost three-fourths of the officers said civilian leaders had given the military “unreasonable goals” in Iraq after Saddam Hussein’s fall. The survey said they believed more troops should have been deployed at the beginning of the war and that dissolving the Iraqi military was an error.

Nevertheless, nearly 90 percent said the surge and Gen. David Petraeus’ counterinsurgency strategy were improving the likelihood that the U.S. military would succeed in Iraq.

The officers also said they believed that either China or Iran — rather than the United States — was becoming the strategic winner of the Iraq war.

Kurt Campbell, who led the organization that carried out the survey, said the United States had been distracted from Asia. He noted that China’s growing global influence began before the Iraq war, but said it forms part of a broader contest in Asia over influence and relationships. According to Campbell, the U.S. concentration on Iraq signals to allies and others that Washington may not be fully focused on developments in Asia.

The report said Iran had benefited from the Iraq war because Iraq had been removed as a “strategic counterweight.”

The survey listed Iran, the Taiwan Strait — where tensions between China and Taiwan have risen — Syria, and North Korea as four possible flashpoints. Officers were asked how prepared the United States would be to successfully carry out a major combat operation in each location.

Respondents rated U.S. preparedness on a scale from 1 to 10, with 10 meaning “fully prepared” and 1 meaning “unable to execute.” Iran received a rating of 4.5; the Taiwan Strait, where China-Taiwan tensions have existed, was rated 4.9; Syria received 5.1; and North Korea was rated 4.7.

The officers gave the highest readiness scores to the Navy and Air Force, at 6.8 and 6.6 respectively. The Army and Marine Corps, which have carried most of the load in Iraq and Afghanistan, were rated lower, at 4.7 and 5.7 respectively.

Other findings from the survey included:

This reflects a broader concern that ongoing commitments in Iraq and Afghanistan have limited the military’s flexibility and reduced its ability to handle new crises.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a CNN-style news article about a Foreign Policy/CNAS survey of U.S. military officers saying the Iraq war has stretched the military dangerously thin and reduced readiness for another major conflict.
counterfactuals.output:
**Survey: Officers say Iraq war has left U.S. military dangerously stretched**

WASHINGTON (CNN-style) — A majority of U.S. military officers say the war in Iraq has strained the armed forces to a dangerous degree and reduced the nation’s ability to respond to another major conflict, according to a survey conducted by *Foreign Policy* magazine and the Center for a New American Security.

The survey found deep concern among officers about the pace of deployments, the condition of equipment and the military’s readiness after years of combat operations in Iraq and Afghanistan. Many respondents said the force has been stretched thin by repeated tours and heavy demands on ground troops, particularly the Army and Marine Corps.

According to the findings, officers expressed doubts that the United States could quickly and effectively handle a new large-scale war without significant strain. The results point to worries inside the military that current commitments have consumed manpower, worn down equipment and limited time for training needed to prepare for conventional conflicts.

The survey comes amid ongoing debate in Washington over the long-term costs of the Iraq war and the size and structure of the U.S. military. Defense officials have repeatedly acknowledged the strain caused by repeated deployments, while also maintaining that U.S. forces remain capable of meeting the country’s security commitments.

Military analysts say the concerns are not limited to troop numbers. Readiness also depends on maintenance, training, rest time between deployments and the ability of units to prepare for missions beyond counterinsurgency operations.

The findings underscore a broader question facing Pentagon leaders and policymakers: whether the armed forces can sustain current operations while preserving the ability to respond to unexpected crises elsewhere in the world.

The survey by *Foreign Policy* and CNAS reflects the views of officers with firsthand experience in the force during wartime, offering a window into internal concerns about the cumulative effects of prolonged conflict.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize the findings of the U.S. Military Index survey of 3,400 current and former officers on Iraq, Afghanistan, military readiness, morale, and potential threats from Iran, China, Syria, and North Korea.
counterfactuals.output:
The **U.S. Military Index** survey of roughly **3,400 current and former U.S. military officers** found a force deeply worried about the effects of the Iraq and Afghanistan wars on U.S. military power, even while retaining confidence in the professionalism and morale of service members.

Key findings:

- **Iraq:** Officers were broadly pessimistic about the Iraq war’s effects on the military. Many believed the war had badly overstretched U.S. ground forces, consumed readiness, and reduced the country’s ability to respond to other crises. Iraq was seen as a major reason the armed forces were weaker than they had been several years earlier.

- **Afghanistan:** Afghanistan was generally viewed as important but under-resourced compared with Iraq. Officers tended to see the mission there as strategically significant, but they expressed concern that U.S. attention and forces had been diverted by Iraq, making success harder.

- **Military readiness:** A central finding was that officers believed U.S. military readiness had declined. They cited repeated deployments, equipment wear, shortages in ground forces, and insufficient dwell time at home. Many thought the military would have difficulty handling another major conflict without significant strain.

- **Morale:** Despite readiness problems, officers reported that morale and professionalism within the ranks remained relatively strong. However, they also warned that repeated combat tours, stress on families, and retention pressures could damage morale over time.

- **Iran:** Iran was viewed as one of the most serious near-term threats, especially because of its nuclear ambitions, regional influence, and potential to destabilize Iraq and the Persian Gulf. Officers were concerned about a confrontation but were wary of opening another war.

- **China:** China was seen less as an immediate battlefield threat and more as the most important long-term strategic competitor. Officers worried about China’s military modernization, its regional ambitions, and the possibility of future conflict over Taiwan or broader Pacific security.

- **Syria:** Syria was generally viewed as a secondary threat compared with Iran, China, or North Korea, but still a destabilizing actor because of its ties to terrorism, influence in Lebanon, and role in the Middle East.

- **North Korea:** North Korea remained a serious concern because of its nuclear program, missiles, unpredictable leadership, and the danger of a crisis on the Korean Peninsula. Officers saw it as a persistent but more geographically contained threat.

Overall, the survey portrayed a military leadership community that respected the force’s competence and morale but believed the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan had left the U.S. military **overextended, less ready, and less able to respond confidently to additional major threats**.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a wire-service report from Washington on a survey showing most military officers believe Iraq has weakened U.S. forces but that the troop surge and Petraeus strategy improved chances of success.
counterfactuals.output:
WASHINGTON (AP) — A majority of U.S. military officers believe the war in Iraq has weakened the armed forces, even as many credit the troop increase and counterinsurgency strategy led by Gen. David Petraeus with improving the chances of success there, according to a new survey.

The findings reflect a conflicted assessment within the officer corps: deep concern that years of combat have strained troops, equipment and readiness, alongside a belief that the 2007 “surge” helped stabilize conditions in Iraq and gave U.S. policy a better prospect of achieving its goals.

Officers surveyed cited repeated deployments, wear on ground forces and the diversion of resources from other security challenges as factors that have left the military less prepared for future conflicts. Many said the Army and Marine Corps in particular have borne the heaviest burden.

At the same time, a significant share said the additional troops sent to Iraq and the shift in tactics under Petraeus — emphasizing population security, cooperation with local leaders and a more aggressive campaign against insurgent networks — had improved the situation on the ground.

The survey suggests that while officers remain skeptical about the long-term costs of the Iraq war, many distinguish between their broader judgment of the conflict and their assessment of the more recent military strategy.

The Bush administration has pointed to reduced violence in Iraq as evidence that the surge is working. Critics, including many Democrats in Congress, argue that tactical gains have not been matched by sufficient political reconciliation among Iraqi factions and that the war has damaged U.S. military readiness.

The poll’s results come as policymakers continue to debate the pace of troop withdrawals and the future U.S. role in Iraq. Military leaders have warned that extended deployments and short dwell times at home have put stress on service members and their families, while limiting time for training and rebuilding units.

Petraeus, who commanded U.S. forces in Iraq during the surge, has said the strategy created conditions for progress but has also cautioned that gains remain fragile.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

The report described survey data from officers indicating broad concern inside the military about readiness. Many officers reportedly believed the armed forces had been weakened by the demands of Iraq, with large numbers saying the war had hurt the military’s ability to fight another major conflict or respond quickly to a new threat.

Michael Boyer, identified in the piece as a military officer, was quoted or paraphrased as expressing concern that the force had become heavily focused on counterinsurgency and stability operations, while losing some capability for broader conventional missions. The article also included comments from Kurt Campbell, a former Pentagon official and foreign-policy expert, who argued that the Iraq war had strategic consequences beyond the Middle East because it consumed U.S. attention and resources.

**U.S. Forces Too Strained to Fight Another Major War, Military Officers Say in Poll**

*By [Reporter Name]*  
*[City], [Date]*

A majority of U.S. military officers believe the armed forces are too stretched to fight another large-scale war, according to a new poll that raises fresh questions about American readiness as the Pentagon manages simultaneous security challenges in Europe, the Middle East and the Indo-Pacific.

The survey, conducted by **[polling organization/publication]** among **[number]** active-duty and retired military officers, found broad concern that years of high operational tempo, recruiting shortfalls, aging equipment and global commitments have left the force under strain. Officers gave mixed readiness marks to the military services and expressed particular concern about the United States’ ability to respond quickly to a major conflict involving **Iran, the Taiwan Strait, Syria or North Korea**.

According to the poll, only **[X percent]** of respondents said U.S. forces are prepared to fight and win another large war while continuing current operations. **[X percent]** said the force is “somewhat unprepared” or “not prepared,” and **[X percent]** said the military could prevail but only at significant cost or after a delayed mobilization.

The findings come as U.S. forces remain engaged in a wide range of missions: supporting Ukraine’s defense against Russia, deterring Iran and its proxy forces in the Middle East, conducting operations against extremist groups in Syria and Iraq, maintaining a naval presence near the Red Sea and Persian Gulf, and preparing for a possible crisis involving China or North Korea.

### Service-by-service readiness concerns

Officers surveyed rated the readiness of the individual services unevenly:

- **Army:** **[X percent / rating]** rated the Army as ready for a major war, while **[X percent]** rated it as strained or underprepared. Respondents cited recruiting problems, ammunition stockpiles, air-defense shortfalls and the demands of deployments to Europe and the Middle East.

- **Marine Corps:** **[X percent / rating]** said the Marine Corps is well positioned for crisis response, particularly in the Indo-Pacific, but others warned that its recent restructuring has reduced some traditional capabilities, including armor and artillery capacity.

- **Navy:** **[X percent / rating]** rated the Navy’s readiness as adequate or strong, though many pointed to ship maintenance delays, overworked crews and insufficient numbers of vessels to meet simultaneous demands in the Pacific, Middle East and Mediterranean.

- **Air Force:** **[X percent / rating]** described the Air Force as capable but stretched, with concerns focused on aging aircraft, pilot retention, munitions stockpiles and the ability to sustain high-intensity operations against a major adversary.

The poll found that officers generally retained confidence in the quality of U.S. troops and commanders, but were less confident in the military’s capacity to sustain a prolonged conflict while maintaining current global commitments.

“This is not a question of whether American service members are capable,” one officer quoted in the survey said. “It is a question of whether we have enough trained people, enough modern equipment, enough ships, enough aircraft and enough ammunition to handle more than one crisis at a time.”

### Regional flashpoints

The survey also asked officers to assess U.S. readiness for several potential conflict scenarios.

#### Iran

On a possible conflict with **Iran**, officers gave the U.S. military a **[rating / X percent confidence level]**. Many respondents said U.S. forces in the region could conduct strikes, defend bases and protect shipping lanes, but warned that a wider war could quickly tax air-defense systems, naval assets and logistics networks.

Several officers noted that Iran’s use of missiles, drones and proxy forces could make a conflict more complex than past U.S. operations in the region.

#### Taiwan Strait

The **Taiwan Strait** drew some of the poll’s most serious concern. Only **[X percent]** of officers said the United States is fully prepared for a major conflict involving China over Taiwan, while **[X percent]** said readiness is insufficient.

Respondents pointed to the distance of the theater, China’s growing missile forces, the size of the Chinese navy and the difficulty of sustaining U.S. forces across the Pacific. Officers also cited shortfalls in shipbuilding, long-range fires, air defense, submarines, logistics and hardened bases.

A conflict over Taiwan, one respondent said, would be “the hardest fight the U.S. military has faced in generations.”

#### Syria

For **Syria**, officers rated U.S. readiness at **[rating / X percent]**, generally viewing the mission as manageable at current levels but vulnerable to escalation. U.S. troops in Syria continue to support operations against the Islamic State while facing threats from Iranian-backed militias and other armed groups.

Respondents warned that a sudden increase in attacks on U.S. personnel could require reinforcements, more air-defense systems or expanded strikes, all of which would compete with other global priorities.

#### North Korea

The poll showed **[X percent]** confidence in U.S. readiness for a renewed conflict with **North Korea**, but many officers said such a war would carry enormous risks. Respondents cited North Korea’s artillery, missiles, cyber capabilities and nuclear arsenal, as well as the challenge of evacuating civilians and sustaining operations on the Korean Peninsula.

Officers generally expressed confidence in the U.S.-South Korea alliance but warned that a major Korean conflict would demand large numbers of ground, air and naval forces at a time when the U.S. military is already stretched.

### Recruiting, munitions and maintenance

Across the survey, officers repeatedly identified several readiness problems: recruiting shortfalls, retention pressures, aging platforms, delayed maintenance, insufficient industrial capacity and limited stocks of precision-guided munitions.

The Army and Navy have faced particularly public recruiting and retention challenges in recent years, while the Air Force has struggled with pilot shortages and the cost of maintaining older aircraft. The Navy has also been under pressure from extended deployments and shipyard backlogs.

The poll’s respondents said the defense industrial base may be unable to produce weapons and replacement parts quickly enough in a prolonged conflict. The war in Ukraine has already exposed limits in U.S. and allied production of artillery shells, air-defense interceptors and other key munitions.

### Pentagon response

Pentagon officials have repeatedly said the U.S. military remains the most capable fighting force in the world and is prepared to meet its obligations. Defense leaders have also emphasized new investments in shipbuilding, long-range missiles, air defense, cyber capabilities, space systems and munitions production.

In recent budget requests, the Defense Department has prioritized modernization aimed at deterring China, while also funding operations in Europe and the Middle East. Officials argue that alliances with NATO, Japan, South Korea, Australia and other partners multiply U.S. strength.

Still, the poll suggests that many officers believe the gap between U.S. commitments and available forces is widening.

### Political implications

The findings are likely to fuel debate in Washington over defense spending, military modernization and the scope of U.S. commitments abroad. Some lawmakers argue the poll shows the need for a larger defense budget and faster weapons production. Others say it highlights the risks of overextension and the need to prioritize threats.

The survey also arrives during a presidential election cycle in which foreign policy and military readiness have become major issues. Conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East, along with China’s military buildup, have sharpened questions about whether the United States can deter multiple adversaries at once.

For officers who responded to the poll, the central concern was not whether the United States could fight a war, but whether it could fight the kind of war its strategy says it must be prepared to win.

“The U.S. military can still deliver overwhelming power,” one respondent said. “But readiness is not unlimited. If we are asking the force to be everywhere, all the time, against every threat, something is going to break.”
